title: Statics & Mechanics of Materials
description: Equilibrium, internal loads, stress, strain, and failure criteria as tools for safe devices, fixtures, implants, and bioreactor hardware.

modifications: Expanded week 1 with free-body diagram boundaries, pin/roller/fixed support models, planar force and moment equations, simply supported beam reactions, distributed-load resultants, and determinacy and unit checks. Clarified both objectives and linked them and the unchanged practice assessment to outcome 1.

Expanded week 3 with average axial stress, engineering strain, uniaxial Hooke's law, elastic extension and stiffness, segmented-bar reasoning, unit checks, and explicit geometry, boundary-condition, material-response and small-strain limits. Clarified both objectives and linked them and the unchanged practice assessment to outcomes 2 and 3. Added an MIT OpenCourseWare Mechanics & Materials I lecture-notes page as a link-only technical reference.

Expanded week 4 with elastic torsional shear in circular shafts, polar second moments for solid and hollow sections, elementary beam-bending stress and rectangular section moments, worked unit checks, geometry sensitivity, and explicit model boundaries. Clarified both objectives and linked them to outcomes 2 and 3. Corrected the preserved beam-bending check's objective association and added one formative torsion-stress calculation, giving both objectives direct practice evidence. Added an MIT OpenCourseWare Mechanics & Materials I lecture-notes page as a link-only technical reference.

Expanded week 8 with distinct yield, ultimate-strength, fracture, fatigue and functional-failure definitions; capacity-to-demand margin calculations; distinctions between strength and pre-factored allowables; and limitations of deterministic factors under uncertainty and cyclic service. Clarified both objectives and linked them and the unchanged-formative arithmetic checks to outcome 4. Corrected the existing factor-of-safety check's objective association and added a formative failure-criteria discrimination item. Added an MIT OpenCourseWare Mechanics & Materials I lecture-notes page as a link-only technical reference.

Extended week 3 with a synthetic parallel-bar compatibility example that combines equilibrium, shared displacement and elastic member stiffness; added a directly mapped objective, three formative checks and three retrieval cards. The schedule remains 14 weeks and examples remain synthetic, with no real-component design guidance.

outcomes.description: Compute axial, torsional, and bending stress.
Relate material response to boundary conditions.
Use safety factors with an explicit failure criterion.

lesson_objectives.description: Draw a free-body diagram for a stated planar beam with external loads and reactions consistent with ideal support models.
Solve a determinate two-dimensional beam reaction problem using signed force and moment balance.
Compute average axial stress and estimate elastic extension for a stated uniform bar.
Check units and evaluate whether the stated geometry, boundary conditions, and material response support a linear-elastic axial estimate.
Resolve load sharing in a redundant axial assembly using equilibrium, displacement compatibility, and elastic force–deformation relations.
Calculate nominal elastic shear stress in a solid or hollow circular shaft from torque and section geometry.
Use bending moment and the correct area second moment to estimate extreme-fiber normal stress in a slender beam.
Distinguish yield, ultimate strength, fracture, fatigue, and functional failure as criteria under a stated load history and requirement.
Calculate and interpret a capacity-to-demand factor for an explicitly stated failure criterion, distinguishing strength from pre-factored allowable.
Compute the second moment of area of a hollow circular section and the maximum bending stress from a moment.
Combine axial and bending stresses at a point and calculate a safety factor against a stated failure criterion.
Explain why a hollow section is more efficient in bending than a solid one of equal area, and evaluate the limits of applying beam theory to bone and implants.
Draw a free-body diagram for a body segment and apply force and moment equilibrium to find unknown muscle and joint forces.
Resolve an angled muscle force into components and compute the resulting joint compression.
Interpret mechanical advantage and evaluate how changes in geometry and load affect muscle and joint forces.
Compute the local stress at a hole or notch from a stress concentration factor and the nominal stress.
Use the elliptical-hole and notch relations to see how the geometry of the root controls the concentration.
Evaluate when a stress concentration matters for static and for fatigue loading, and how to reduce it.
Compute the stress amplitude, mean stress and stress ratio of a cycle.
Use Basquin's law to estimate life at a stress amplitude and how it responds to small changes in stress.
Apply a mean-stress correction and Miner's rule, and evaluate their limits and the scatter of fatigue data.
Compute the second moment of area, radius of gyration and slenderness ratio of a solid circular strut.
Use Euler's formula with an effective-length factor to find the critical load and critical stress, and see how they scale with length and diameter.
Decide whether elastic buckling or yielding governs a given strut, and size a strut for a design load.
Compute the principal stresses, their orientation and the maximum in-plane shear stress for a plane stress state.
Use the stress-transformation equations to find the stress on an inclined plane.
Compare the von Mises and Tresca criteria for a ductile material and state what they do not cover.
Compute the second moment of area of a rectangular section and use the standard formulas to find the deflection and stiffness of cantilever and simply supported beams.
Obtain a flexural modulus and the maximum stress from three-point bending data.
Evaluate how thickness and span control stiffness, and when the simple beam formulas are not valid.
Compute the probability of failure of a brittle part under uniform stress from the Weibull distribution and invert it to find a design stress.
Estimate the Weibull modulus from ranked strength data and interpret it as a measure of scatter.
Evaluate how the stressed volume changes the strength (the weakest-link size effect) and when the model does not apply.
Summarize fatigue lives by stress amplitude, counting failures and run-outs and averaging the logarithm of the life.
Fit a Basquin line to the level means and read the exponent and a predicted life from it.
Evaluate how scatter, censoring and extrapolation limit what fatigue data support.
Explain why a scaffold that meets a static strength target can fail under cyclic perfusion, using stress amplification, fatigue life and stiffness loss.
Estimate the number of cycles in a service period, the strut stress amplitude, the fatigue life and the effect of a loss of strength.
Design an accelerated test with controls and stopping criteria, and bound the heating that acceleration introduces.
Solve support reactions and section-resultant balance for a simply supported beam under distributed or concentrated transverse loading.
Construct piecewise shear-force and bending-moment functions from cut-section equilibrium and load–shear–moment relationships; verify jumps and support conditions.
Locate a candidate maximum bending moment and use a stated cross-section to estimate nominal elastic bending stress with consistent units and assumptions.
Use Poisson's ratio and the generalized Hooke's law to calculate normal strains from a multiaxial stress state, including lateral contraction and volume change.
Calculate thermal strain, the stress in a fully or partly constrained member, and the stress induced by a lateral constraint.
Derive and apply hoop and axial stresses in thin-walled cylinders and spheres, calculate the change in radius, and state when the thin-wall model applies.

duration.equivalent_structure: Proposed 14-week undergraduate scope only. The opening week groups free-body diagrams with a short body-equilibrium application; week 2 develops beam load, shear, and moment diagrams before stress. The four compact prototype readings in weeks 1, 3, 4 and 8 now have expanded instruction beside original lessons on body equilibrium, beam loading, bone bending, beam deflection, combined stress, multiaxial strain and pressure vessels, stress concentrations, buckling, fatigue and brittle strength. Week 12 is a synthetic-data fatigue-life lab, and week 14 pairs failure analysis with the course case. All activities are open, ungraded practice. No graded homework sets, exams or project is present, and workload is unmeasured; this is not evidence of semester equivalence.

weeks.title: Equilibrium: free-body diagrams and force/moment balance
Distributed loads, shear force, and bending moment
Axial load, stress, strain, and compatibility
Bending of a long bone: second moment of area and combined stresses
Beam deflection and stiffness: three-point bending and the flexural modulus
Combined stress and strain: principal stresses, Mohr's circle, yield, multiaxial Hooke's law and pressure vessels
Stress concentrations: holes, notches and local stress
Buckling of slender struts: Euler load, effective length and slenderness
Fatigue under cyclic loading: S–N curves, mean stress and cumulative damage
Virtual lab: fatigue lives, scatter and run-outs
Strength of brittle materials: flaws, scatter and the Weibull distribution
Why a scaffold that meets its strength target can still collapse: failure analysis and an accelerated test plan

lessons.title: Free-body diagrams and equilibrium
lessons.worked_example: A simply supported 4.0 m beam has a 200 N downward load 1.0 m from the left support. Taking moments there gives the right reaction as 200×1.0/4.0=50 N; vertical force balance then gives 150 N at the left support.

modules.title: Axial load, stress, strain, and compatibility

lessons.title: Axial load, stress, strain, and compatibility
lessons.worked_example: For a 100 mm uniform bar with A=10 mm², E=2 GPa=2,000 N/mm², and F=20 N, σ=F/A=2 MPa, ε=σ/E=0.001, and ΔL=εL=0.1 mm; equivalently, k=AE/L=200 N/mm and F/k=0.1 mm. In a separate synthetic parallel-bar assembly with equal 400 mm lengths and 100 mm² areas, moduli 200 and 100 GPa, and 30 kN total load, compatibility gives 0.4 mm common extension and a 20/10 kN force split. Both examples assume uniform linear-elastic axial behavior.

lessons.title: Torsion and bending
lessons.worked_example: For a 20 mm solid circular shaft under 12 N·m, J=πd⁴/32=1.571×10⁻⁸ m⁴ and τmax=Tc/J=7.64 MPa. For the preserved rectangular-beam example, b=0.050 m, h=0.100 m, M=500 N·m, I=bh³/12=4.167×10⁻⁶ m⁴, and σmax=Mc/I=6.00 MPa at the extreme fibers. Both results assume the stated ideal elastic models and consistent SI units.

modules.title: Failure criteria, fatigue, and design margins

lessons.title: Failure criteria, fatigue, and design margins
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic member with stated capacity 900 N and modeled design demand 300 N has n=900/300=3 under the chosen failure criterion. The units cancel. This deterministic ratio is not a probability and does not account for omitted load, strength, or model uncertainty.

lessons.title: Bending of a long bone: second moment of area, combined stresses and why bones are hollow
lessons.worked_example: For r_o = 13 mm and r_i = 7 mm, I = 20546 mm⁴; 100 N·m gives 63.3 MPa bending stress, plus 5.31 MPa from a 2000 N axial load, so 68.6 MPa and a safety factor of 2.19 against 150 MPa; a solid rod of equal area would reach 96.9 MPa.

lessons.title: Force and moment equilibrium in the body: free-body diagrams of a forearm holding a load
lessons.worked_example: Moments about the elbow give a muscle force of 493.8 N for a 50 N load at 35 cm, and the joint pushes down with 428.8 N; at 80° the muscle needs 501.4 N and adds 87.1 N of compression; mechanical advantage 0.114.

modules.title: Distributed loads, shear force, and bending moment

lessons.title: Distributed loads, shear force, and bending moment
lessons.worked_example: For a simply supported 6 m beam with a full-span 2 kN/m load, reactions are 6 kN each, V(x)=6−2x kN, M(x)=6x−x² kN·m, and Mmax=9 kN·m at x=3 m. A 0.10 m × 0.20 m rectangular section has I=6.667×10⁻⁵ m⁴ and nominal extreme-fiber stress 13.5 MPa.

lessons.title: Stress concentrations: holes, notches and why the nominal stress is not the stress that fails a part
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic plate with a far-field stress of 90 MPa and a hole with K_t 2.5 has a peak stress of 225 MPa (first yield at 80 MPa far-field), an elliptical slot with semi-axes 1.5 mm and 0.75 mm has K_t 5, and a 0.8 mm notch with a 0.2 mm root has K_t 5.00 and K_f 3.40; in the lesson a 3-fold concentration puts a 50 MPa far-field stress at 150 MPa, above a 120 MPa yield strength.

lessons.title: Fatigue under cyclic loading: S–N curves, Basquin's law, mean stress and cumulative damage
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic material with σ_f′ 800 MPa and b −0.12 lasts 8,101 cycles at 250 MPa and 52,016 at 200 MPa, so 2,000 cycles at the first and 15,000 at the second use 54% of its life (Miner's sum 0.535); in the lesson, a cycle between 200 and 20 MPa has amplitude 90 MPa, mean 110 MPa and R = 0.1, and a 10% lower amplitude multiplies the life by 2.87.

lessons.title: Buckling of slender struts: Euler's critical load, effective length and slenderness
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic strut with d 0.8 mm, L 6 mm, E 1500 MPa and one end fixed, one pinned has slenderness 21, below the transition value 22.21 for a yield stress of 30 MPa, so it yields at 15.08 N before the Euler value of 16.87 N; in the lesson a pinned strut of d 0.5 mm and L 5 mm has an Euler load of 2.422 N and slenderness 40.

lessons.title: Combined stress: principal stresses, Mohr's circle and yield criteria
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic state of 60, −20 and 35 MPa has principal stresses 73.15 and −33.15 MPa at 20.6°, a von Mises stress of 94.21 MPa and factors of safety 1.592 (von Mises) and 1.411 (Tresca) for a yield stress of 150 MPa; in the lesson the state 80, 20, 30 MPa has R = 42.43 MPa and a von Mises stress of 88.88 MPa.

modules.title: Multiaxial Hooke's law, thermal strain and thin-walled pressure vessels

lessons.title: Multiaxial Hooke's law, thermal strain and thin-walled pressure vessels
lessons.worked_example: A tank of radius 0.30 m at 1.5 MPa with a 120 MPa allowable hoop stress needs t ≥ 3.75 mm (r/t = 80). Then σ_θ = 120 MPa, σ_z = 60 MPa and the absolute maximum shear is 60 MPa; with E = 200 GPa and ν = 0.30, ε_θ = 5.1 × 10⁻⁴, ε_z = 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ and the enclosed volume grows by 1.14 × 10⁻³.

lessons.title: Beam deflection and stiffness: three-point bending, superposition and what the span and thickness control
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic strip with b 4 mm, h 0.8 mm, span 16 mm and E 2400 MPa deflects 0.2708 mm under a central load of 1.3 N (stiffness 4.80 N/mm, stress 12.19 MPa) and would need a thickness of 1.022 mm for 10 N/mm; in the lesson, a strip with span 20 mm, b 5 mm, h 1 mm and E 3000 MPa deflects 0.2667 mm under 2 N.

lessons.title: Strength of brittle materials: flaws, scatter and the Weibull distribution
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic ceramic with σ₀ 120 MPa and m 8 has a failure probability of 0.0953 at 90 MPa, needs 61.9 MPa for a 0.5% probability and only 41.0 MPa when the volume is 27 times larger; in the lesson, σ₀ 100 MPa and m 10 give a failure probability of 0.1018 at 80 MPa and 63.13 MPa for 1%.

lessons.title: Virtual lab 1: fatigue lives, scatter and run-outs
lessons.worked_example: In the synthetic fatigue data the standard deviation of log10 life at 260 MPa is 0.183, the fitted slope of mean log10 life on log10 stress is −10.15 (b = −0.099), counting the two run-outs at 200 MPa as failures at the cutoff raises the mean log10 life from 6.108 to 6.185, and the median life predicted at 160 MPa is an extrapolation.

lessons.title: Why a scaffold that meets its strength target can still collapse: a failure analysis and an accelerated test plan
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic scaffold with a strut stress amplitude of 5.25 MPa and σ_f′ 28 MPa has a fatigue life of 59.8 million cycles, a margin of 23.1 over the 2,592,000 cycles required, falling to 3.8 after a 15% loss of strength, and an adiabatic heating bound of 3.53 mK/s at 10 Hz; in the lesson, the scaffold with a 1.9 MPa yield strength has a strut life of 7.49 million cycles against 2,592,000 required.

grading_policy.attempt_policy: Unlimited formative retries; no summative grade is awarded.
grading_policy.solution_release: Public practice solutions may be shown after an attempt. They are not production exam keys.
grading_policy.late_policy: No deadlines or late penalties exist in this partial package.
grading_policy.appeals: No instructor review workflow is implemented; report ambiguous practice items to repository maintainers.

accessibility.diagram_policy: The seed package contains no imported diagrams; newly authored diagrams require descriptions and individual license tracking.
known_issues: Unicode equations require structured mathematical alternatives and assistive-technology review.

history.summary: Preserved original compact prototype content in separate manifests and readings; labeled partial without semester or credit equivalency.

Added an original lesson on bending of a long bone (second moment of area, combined stresses, safety factor, hollow sections and stress shielding) with synthetic data, formative items with computed keys and retrieval cards. The package remains partial and unreviewed.

Added an original lesson on force and moment equilibrium of a forearm holding a load with synthetic data, formative items with computed keys and retrieval cards. The package remains partial and unreviewed.

Assessments with items now also list the course outcomes those items assess, derived from each item's lesson objective and that objective's outcome links. The rubric-only case lists none, and neither do the 4 prototype-unit assessments, whose objectives are not yet linked to an outcome. No readings, items or keys changed. The syllabus was regenerated from the manifest: it states the current version, lists every lesson with its item and card counts, and describes the current practice and limitations (it still described only the four original units). The course limitations shown to learners were also updated: they still described one formative check per lesson and the original numerical rules. The package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Fixed number formatting that an earlier authoring step left in learner-visible text: raw exponent notation (a number written with the letter e and a power of ten) and floating-point artifacts (a decimal with a long run of trailing digits) in item statics-materials-3:bending-stress. No answer key, tolerance or objective changed. The package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

Added a proposed 14-week schedule; seven original lessons (stress concentrations; fatigue, S-N curves and cumulative damage; buckling of slender struts; principal stresses, Mohr's circle and yield criteria; beam deflection and the flexural modulus; brittle strength and the Weibull distribution; and a failure analysis and accelerated test plan, which prepares the course case on a scaffold that collapses under cyclic perfusion); and a synthetic-data lab on fatigue lives, scatter and run-outs. No new references were added. All activities remain ungraded practice; the package remains partial and unreviewed, gives no design basis, test protocol or safety advice, and makes no claim about any device, material or person.

The course remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

limitations: All four legacy prototype readings now have expanded instruction beside the original lessons and one synthetic-data virtual lab; the package still is not equivalent to a full university semester.

A proposed 14-week schedule exists but is unmeasured and unreviewed. There is one synthetic-data virtual lab and no substantive homework sequence, laboratory sequence, midterm or cumulative final. An inactive integrative project draft is not scheduled or graded.

Practice items are short formative checks (two to five per prototype unit and six to eleven per original lesson); they do not demonstrate comprehensive outcome coverage or mastery, and objective associations remain provisional.
Bloom labels and structured prerequisite edges are initial authoring classifications awaiting subject-matter review.
Question answers and solution feedback are intentionally public practice authoring specifications, not restricted exam keys.

Of the 92 numerical answers in this package, 46 require a unit, one checks significant figures and none checks dimensions; the others accept a number within a stated tolerance, with the unit optional.
Total workload and weekly duration are unknown; former nominal credit values and hardcoded reading times do not establish workload.

All loads, materials, specimens and numbers are synthetic teaching examples; this package gives no design basis, test protocol or safety advice and says nothing about any real device, implant or person. The models are simplified textbook descriptions, not analysis methods for real components. The compatibility example does not resolve truss, beam or real assembly design.
intentionally_omitted: Graded assessments, an activated integrative project and a laboratory sequence are not authored yet (one synthetic-data virtual lab exists); the original lessons extend a partial package.
